# Summary

This is a Project Gutenberg eBook edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's classic novella *The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde*, originally released June 27, 2008 (eBook #43) and most recently updated May 12, 2026. The text is freely available in English under Project Gutenberg's licensing terms with minimal restrictions. The work is divided into ten chapters: "Story of the Door," "Search for Mr. Hyde," "Dr. Jekyll Was Quite at Ease," "The Carew Murder Case," "Incident of the Letter," "Incident of Dr. Lanyon," "Incident at the Window," "The Last Night," "Dr. Lanyon's Narrative," and "Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case," which together compose Stevenson's famous tale exploring the duality of human nature.

# Summary

In this opening section of *The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde*, lawyer Mr. Utterson—an austere, emotionally reserved but fundamentally good man—takes his Sunday walk with his distant kinsman Richard Enfield through a London street. They encounter a sinister, neglected door that prompts Enfield to recount a disturbing incident: he witnessed a small man named Hyde callously trample a young girl, and when confronted, Hyde was forced to pay compensation of nearly one hundred pounds via a check signed by a prominent, respectable gentleman. Enfield reveals that Hyde used a key to access the building behind the mysterious door, suggesting connection between the man of good repute and the morally repugnant Hyde. Utterson, already knowing the identity of the check's drawer, appears deeply troubled by the revelation, and the two agree never to discuss the matter again.

# Summary

Mr. Utterson, a lawyer, becomes deeply troubled after reviewing Dr. Jekyll's will, which leaves all his possessions to the mysterious Edward Hyde, and grants Hyde full control should Jekyll disappear for three months. Disturbed by this arrangement and having recently learned of Hyde's involvement in a violent incident, Utterson seeks information from their mutual friend Dr. Lanyon, who reveals he has not seen Jekyll in over a decade due to Jekyll's "unscientific" pursuits. Unable to learn anything about Hyde from Lanyon, Utterson begins nightly vigils outside Jekyll's house and eventually encounters the small, plainly-dressed Hyde entering through a side door. Though repulsed by Hyde's appearance and manner, Utterson obtains his Soho address. Later visiting Jekyll's home, Utterson learns from the butler Poole that Hyde has a key and free access to the laboratory. Deeply troubled by these discoveries, Utterson suspects Jekyll is being blackmailed or ruined by Hyde, fearing the will may motivate Hyde to hasten Jekyll's demise to claim his inheritance.

# Summary

During a dinner at Dr. Jekyll's home, Mr. Utterson remains behind with the doctor to discuss his troubling will, which benefits the mysterious Edward Hyde. When Utterson expresses concern about what he has learned of Hyde's abominable behavior, Jekyll becomes visibly distressed but refuses to explain the situation, claiming it cannot be mended by talking. Despite Utterson's offers to help, Jekyll insists the matter is private and cryptically states he can rid himself of Hyde whenever he chooses. Nevertheless, Jekyll asks Utterson to promise to protect Hyde's interests and ensure he receives his rights should something happen to Jekyll, which the reluctant lawyer finally agrees to do.

# The Carew Murder Case Summary

In October, London is shocked by the brutal murder of the distinguished Sir Danvers Carew. A maid witnesses the crime from her window: an elderly gentleman with white hair is savagely attacked and beaten to death by a small man she recognizes as Mr. Hyde, who uses a heavy cane as a weapon. When the body is discovered, lawyer Mr. Utterson identifies the victim and recognizes the broken cane as one he had given to Henry Jekyll years ago. Utterson directs Inspector Newcomen to Hyde's residence in the disreputable Soho district. They find Hyde's rooms ransacked, with burned papers and the other half of the cane hidden behind the door. A green cheque book and substantial funds at the bank under Hyde's name provide further evidence. Though the inspector is confident in capturing Hyde, he proves difficult to apprehend because he has few associates, has never been photographed, and those who have seen him describe him inconsistently—though all agree he carries an inexplicable sense of deformity.

# Summary

When lawyer Utterson visits Dr. Jekyll at his laboratory following the murder of Sir Danvers Carew, he finds the doctor looking deathly ill. Jekyll reveals he has received a letter from Edward Hyde, assuring him of his safety and escape, which he asks Utterson to evaluate regarding police disclosure. Though the letter reassures Utterson about Jekyll's involvement, he later discovers it was delivered through the laboratory door rather than by post. That evening, Utterson shows the letter to his trusted head clerk Guest under the guise of seeking his expertise in handwriting analysis. Guest makes a shocking discovery: the letter's handwriting closely resembles Dr. Jekyll's own handwriting from an invitation note. Deeply disturbed by this revelation that Jekyll may have forged the letter for the murderer Hyde, Utterson locks the documents away, his trust in his friend severely shaken.

# Summary

Following Sir Danvers Carew's murder and Mr. Hyde's mysterious disappearance, Mr. Utterson observes Dr. Jekyll's initial recovery and return to social life. However, this peace is disrupted when Jekyll suddenly withdraws from society around January 12th. When Utterson visits Dr. Lanyon, he finds him mortally ill and deeply disturbed, refusing any mention of Jekyll and declaring himself a "doomed man." Jekyll's response to Utterson's inquiries reveals he has imposed strict self-seclusion due to an unnamed "punishment and danger," begging for silence and understanding. Dr. Lanyon dies shortly thereafter, leaving Utterson a sealed envelope with cryptic instructions to open it only upon Jekyll's death or disappearance—a phrase that alarms Utterson given its connection to Hyde and Jekyll's original will. Despite his mounting curiosity and concern, Utterson respects these wishes, though his visits to Jekyll's increasingly isolated household become less frequent as the doctor retreats into his laboratory, appearing troubled and silent.

# Summary

During a Sunday walk through a by-street with Mr. Enfield, Mr. Utterson expresses concern about Dr. Jekyll and suggests visiting him. They find Jekyll sitting at a window of his house, appearing dejected and reluctant to join them. When Utterson and Enfield propose conversing from the courtyard below, Jekyll initially agrees but suddenly displays an expression of such profound terror and despair that it horrifies both men. Jekyll abruptly slams the window shut, leaving Utterson and Enfield deeply shaken and silent as they depart, both pale and visibly disturbed by the mysterious incident.

# Combined Summary

On a cold March evening, butler Poole alerts lawyer Utterson to a crisis at Dr. Jekyll's house. Upon investigation, they find the servants terrified and Jekyll locked in his cabinet for a week, ordering rare chemicals and rejecting impure samples. When Poole glimpses the figure inside, he recognizes not Jekyll but a dwarf-like creature resembling Mr. Hyde—Jekyll's associate connected to a previous murder. Though a voice claims to be Jekyll's, Poole insists otherwise. Utterson and Poole force open the cabinet door, discovering Edward Hyde's poisoned corpse but no sign of Jekyll. Among the papers on Jekyll's desk, they find a dated note in Jekyll's handwriting and a new will naming Utterson. Jekyll's letter states he has fled and anticipates an imminent end, instructing Utterson to read narratives from both Lanyon and Jekyll himself that will explain the mystery. Determined to protect Jekyll's reputation by keeping the matter quiet, Utterson returns to his office to read the two accounts before deciding whether to contact the police before midnight.

# Summary of Dr. Lanyon's Narrative

Dr. Lanyon receives an urgent, cryptic letter from his old friend Dr. Henry Jekyll requesting that he retrieve a locked drawer containing powders, a blood-red phial, and a notebook from Jekyll's cabinet and deliver it to a mysterious messenger at midnight. Though puzzled and suspicious of Jekyll's sanity, Lanyon complies, forcing open the cabinet with a locksmith and examining the drawer's contents—which appear to be records of chemical experiments. At midnight, a small, grotesque stranger arrives, collects the drawer, and mixes the red liquid with one of the powders, which transforms into a dark purple then watery green solution. After offering Lanyon a choice between ignorance or witnessing an extraordinary revelation, the stranger drinks the mixture and undergoes a shocking transformation before Lanyon's eyes, revealing himself to be Dr. Jekyll. # Combined Summary

Dr. Jekyll, born to wealth and virtue, develops an internal conflict between his respectable public image and his hidden desires. Through scientific research into humanity's dual nature, he creates a drug that physically separates his good and evil aspects, transforming him into Edward Hyde. Initially able to alternate between forms at will, Jekyll uses this ability to indulge in secret depravities while maintaining his reputation. However, the balance deteriorates as Hyde grows stronger and Jekyll weakens, eventually transforming involuntarily. After committing murder, Jekyll attempts redemption but finds his fundamental duality reasserts itself. The transformations become increasingly involuntary and frequent, with Hyde growing more violent and the drug losing efficacy. When Jekyll's supply of the crucial salt becomes irreplaceable, he realizes he cannot prevent his permanent transformation into Hyde, leading to his final collapse as his evil half consumes him completely.
